# Three-height classification of all median-line simplex sections

This is a structural ordinary simplex theorem in every dimension. It
does not bound the resulting weighted cap mean. It extracts a consequence
of the proved reciprocal-transform lemma in
`candidate 8704554a92158bfc`, independently audited
in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.

## Theorem

Let T be a d-simplex, d>=2. Let y have positive barycentric coordinates

    lambda=(a,b,...,b),    a+d b=1.

Consider any proper hyperplane section of T with centroid y, and let
c_0,...,c_d be raw affine values of its oriented defining margin at the
vertices. Then:

1. No ordinary vertex i>=1 has c_i=0.
2. All positive ordinary coefficients c_i (i>=1) are equal.
3. All negative ordinary coefficients c_i (i>=1) are equal.
4. If c_0=0, then a=1/d; its positive and negative ordinary groups are
   nonempty, and their common values p>0 and -q<0 satisfy
   `k p=(d-k)q`, where k is the number of positive ordinary vertices.

Thus every such section has at most three distinct vertex heights:
the distinguished height c_0, one common positive ordinary height, and
one common negative ordinary height. Empty sign groups are allowed.
The conclusion does not assume y is in the central region a<=1/d.

## 1. Zero vertex heights

If c_i=0, the section is a (d-1)-dimensional pyramid with apex v_i and
base in the opposite face {xi_i=0}. To see this exactly, normalize the
other barycentric coordinates of any section point with xi_i<1 by
1-xi_i. Their raw margin still vanishes, so the normalized point lies
in the section of that opposite face. Conversely the whole join with
v_i lies in the original section. Properness and y in int(T) ensure
the base has dimension d-2. The centroid of this pyramid has apex
barycentric coordinate 1/d. This follows, for example, by slicing at
xi_i=t: cross-sectional (d-2)-volume is proportional to (1-t)^(d-2),
whose normalized mean t is 1/d.

But b=(1-a)/d<1/d. Therefore no ordinary vertex has zero height. If
c_0=0, the same argument forces a=1/d. Positive and negative ordinary
heights both occur because the cut is proper and goes through the
interior. The stated relation then follows from the defining equation
`sum lambda_i c_i=0` after applying Sections 2--3.

## 2. Equal small centroid coordinates have equal positive heights

We recall exactly the proved transform mechanism from the dependency.
Let E_0,...,E_d be independent unit exponentials and set

    W=sum_i c_i E_i,
    P(c)=Pr(W>=0).

Writing E_i=G U_i gives uniform simplex barycentrics U independent
of G. The first-variation identity at a section with centroid lambda
is

    P_i(c)=d f_W(0) lambda_i.                           (1)

Equivalently this follows by differentiating a cap in its vertex
margin values: its gradient is its normalized coarea section mass
times the centroid's barycentric vector. The size-bias formula is

    P_i(c)=f_(W+c_i E')(0),                            (2)

with E' an independent unit exponential.

Choose two positive coefficients c_i,c_j whose centroid coordinates
are equal and at most 1/d. If there are two such coefficients, W has
at least two positive phases and at least one negative phase. The
regularity and log-concavity hypotheses of the audited transform lemma
therefore hold, including zero other coefficients. With the law of W
held fixed, define for t>0

    phi(t)=f_(W+t E')(0)/f_W(0),    psi(t)=1/phi(t).

The dependency proves that psi is convex, psi(0+)=1, and

    psi(t)>=1 implies psi'(t)>0.                      (3)

Equations (1)--(2) give

    psi(c_i)=psi(c_j)=1/(d lambda_i)>=1.

If c_i<c_j, convexity and (3) would imply

    psi(c_j)>=psi(c_i)+(c_j-c_i)psi'(c_i)>psi(c_i),

a contradiction. Hence c_i=c_j. A sign group of size one of course
already has equal heights. This proves assertion 2 because every
ordinary centroid coordinate is b<1/d.

For completeness, the transform's convexity is the elementary
half-line log-concave second-moment calculation: with
h(s)=f_W(-s)/f_W(0), A(t)=integral exp(-s/t)h(s) ds,
we have psi(t)=t/A(t), and

    psi''(t)=[2M_1(t)^2-M_0(t)M_2(t)]/[t^3 M_0(t)^3]>=0.

The moment inequality is `E X^2<=2(E X)^2` for a positive log-concave
half-line density. Its equality case makes h a decreasing exponential,
for which psi is affine with positive slope; otherwise psi is strictly
convex. This supplies strict (3), not merely nondecreasing behavior.
All analytic justifications and the equality case are proved in the
cited audited source; none is a new assumed classification principle.

## 3. Negative heights and the complete scope

Apply Section 2 to the complementary oriented cap, whose coefficients
are -c_i and whose section centroid is still lambda. It proves assertion
3. Together with Section 1 this proves the theorem.

In dimension three this is an alternative analytic explanation of the
equal-height step in
`candidate 7fd42b1082a20d4b`. That
three-dimensional source gives a fully elementary diagonal proof and
then proves the sharp weighted inequality by exact univariate algebra.
The present all-dimensional classification does not import that scalar
inequality into higher dimensions.

## 4. Exact one-variable section law after classification

There is also an explicit finite-integral formulation, which can be
useful without guessing an extremal coefficient pattern. Orient a section
with c_0>0 toward v_0, and suppose k>=1 ordinary vertices are positive
and m=d-k>=1 are negative. Rescale so the common negative value is -1.
Write its margin as

    L=xi_0/A+R/B-1,
    R=sum_(positive ordinary i)xi_i,
    N=sum_(negative ordinary i)xi_i,
    0<A<1, 0<B<1.

On L=0 parameterize

    xi_0=A t,    R=B(1-t),
    N=1-B+(B-A)t,       0<=t<=1.

The induced uniform section law of t has density proportional to

    (1-t)^(k-1) [1-B+(B-A)t]^(m-1).                    (4)

Indeed the uniform simplex pushforward to (xi_0,R,N) has density
proportional to R^(k-1)N^(m-1). Coarea along the displayed affine line
has a constant Jacobian; substitution contributes only a further
constant B^(k-1). The positive affine bracket in (4) has positive
endpoints 1-B and 1-A, so this is a finite positive polynomial density.
The centroid conditions are exactly

    A E[t]=a,
    B(1-E[t])=k b,
    1-B+(B-A)E[t]=m b.                                 (5)

Only two of these are independent, since their sum is one. Conversely
(4)--(5), together with a+d b=1, force the centroid of every individual
ordinary coordinate to be b by within-group permutation symmetry.
Thus (4)--(5) are an exact characterization in this sign pattern, not
an approximation. Vertex-isolating patterns and c_0=0 are already
handled separately above; the case c_0<0 is obtained by reversing the
orientation. No weighted cap lower bound is inferred solely from this
one-variable law.
